title: What is an estuary? Where a river meets the sea

sources.name: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is an estuary?
NOAA Fisheries — Estuary habitat and nurseries of the sea

practice: Keep exploring our planet with a round of General Knowledge.

sections.html:
An estuary is usually a coastal body of water where freshwater from rivers meets and mixes with seawater. Its surrounding wetlands are part of the story too.

A river brings water from the land. The sea brings salt and tides. Where they meet, the landscape can become a shifting mixture of channels, mudflats and marshes. Geography has arranged a rather busy meeting.
sections.title: A meeting place with moving edges

sections.html:
NOAA describes the mixture as brackish water: partly salty, rather than fully fresh or as salty as the open sea.

It is not a permanent recipe. River flow and incoming tides can change the balance. You should not expect a neat line with freshwater on one side and seawater on the other. The meeting is a mixing process.
sections.title: What does brackish mean?

sections.html:
NOAA Fisheries calls estuaries nurseries of the sea. Many animals reproduce or spend their early lives there, finding food and shelter in habitats such as marshes and seagrass beds.

Rising and falling tides change water depth and conditions. For an estuary’s residents, adapting to change is part of living in the neighbourhood.
sections.title: Why so much wildlife?

sections.html:
Not every estuary contains seawater. Freshwater estuaries occur around the Great Lakes, where chemically different river and lake waters meet. Old Woman Creek on Lake Erie is one example.

Follow the water a little further: discover where the ocean gets its salt, or see how a river bend can move. Water is a remarkably restless mapmaker.
sections.title: The freshwater plot twist

description: An estuary is usually where river water meets the sea. Discover brackish water, tidal changes and the surprising estuaries that contain no seawater.

options: Only water below the ocean floor
A mixture of fresh water and salty seawater
questions.explanation: Brackish water is partly salty. In a coastal estuary, river water and seawater can mix.

questions.prompt: Why can an estuary’s saltiness change?
options: River flow and incoming tides can change the mixture
The word estuary changes its meaning every day
All the water stops moving at night
Salt turns into sand every morning
questions.explanation: The river and sea inputs vary, so the mixture need not stay at one fixed saltiness.
